title: Job 28:12–19
context: Job 28:12–19 continues the hymn to wisdom, whose speaker is debated (Job, or the narrator in an interlude). The poem asks where wisdom can be found and answers that humans do not know its worth and do not find it in the land of the living. The deep and the sea say that it is not in them. It cannot be bought with gold, silver, the gold of Ophir, onyx, sapphire, coral, crystal, or the topaz of Ethiopia; its price is above rubies. Some identifications of these precious stones are uncertain; the word rendered sapphire may refer to lapis lazuli. Both traditions agree that the stanza teaches that true wisdom cannot be reached by human effort or bought with any wealth.

verses.text: “But where will wisdom be found? Where is the place of understanding?
verses.arminianNotes: The poem asks where wisdom will be found and where understanding has its place. Arminians see the central question of the hymn, which turns from what humans can dig up to what they cannot find on their own.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the question as exposing the limits of human ability. Both traditions read it as the hinge of the poem, and they note that the same question returns in verse 20 before God gives the answer.

verses.text: Man doesn’t know its price, and it isn’t found in the land of the living.
verses.arminianNotes: Humans do not know its price, and it is not found in the land of the living. Arminian readers see the poem stating plainly that wisdom lies beyond human discovery, however skilled people may be.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as teaching that wisdom must be given rather than found. Both traditions hold this as shared ground, which the poem’s conclusion in verses 23–28 confirms by pointing to God.

verses.text: The deep says, ‘It isn’t in me.’ The sea says, ‘It isn’t with me.’
verses.arminianNotes: The deep and the sea both say that wisdom is not in them. Arminians see creation personified as giving testimony that wisdom is not hidden in any part of the world for people to dig up.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the deep and the sea as the farthest and most mysterious parts of creation. Both traditions read the verse as saying that wisdom is not a natural resource, even in the places humans cannot reach.

verses.text: It can’t be gotten for gold, neither will silver be weighed for its price.
verses.arminianNotes: Wisdom cannot be bought with gold, and silver cannot be weighed out for its price. Arminian readers see the poem turning from searching to buying, and denying that wealth can obtain what searching cannot.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as a warning against trusting riches. Both traditions note that the metals named in verse 1 return here, now shown to be worthless for gaining wisdom.

verses.text: It can’t be valued with the gold of Ophir, with the precious onyx, or the sapphire.
verses.arminianNotes: Wisdom cannot be valued with the gold of Ophir, precious onyx, or sapphire. Arminians see the list of famous treasures growing, each one falling short of wisdom’s worth. The location of Ophir is uncertain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read Ophir as a source of fine gold known elsewhere in the Old Testament. Both traditions treat the list as poetic emphasis rather than a precise inventory, all pointing to wisdom’s surpassing value.

verses.text: Gold and glass can’t equal it, neither will it be exchanged for jewels of fine gold.
verses.arminianNotes: Gold and glass cannot equal wisdom, and it cannot be exchanged for jewels of fine gold. Arminian readers see that in the ancient world glass was itself a costly material, so even rare luxuries cannot match wisdom.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as continuing the poem’s steady point: nothing people prize can be traded for wisdom. Both traditions hold this as shared ground about wisdom’s worth.

verses.text: No mention will be made of coral or of crystal. Yes, the price of wisdom is above rubies.
verses.arminianNotes: No mention is made of coral or crystal, and wisdom’s price is above rubies. Arminians see a line that Proverbs also uses about wisdom (compare Proverbs 3:15 and 8:11), showing that this conviction runs through Scripture’s wisdom books.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the shared theme as part of Scripture’s consistent witness. Both traditions note that the identification of some of these stones is uncertain, but the meaning is clear: wisdom is worth more than any jewel.

verses.text: The topaz of Ethiopia will not equal it. It won’t be valued with pure gold.
verses.arminianNotes: The topaz of Ethiopia cannot equal wisdom, and it cannot be valued with pure gold. Arminian readers see the stanza ending with one more precious stone from a distant land, sealing the point that wisdom cannot be bought.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the closing lines of the stanza as making wisdom’s value plain. Both traditions note that the poem now returns to its question in verse 20, having shown that neither searching nor wealth can obtain wisdom.
